title: Sleep hygiene, caffeine use, and academic performance among university students: A cross-sectional study
content:
by Razi Alshaikh, Wadea Jebriel, Mohammad Shahrouri, Tartil Zarura, Hasan Khouli

Background

Caffeine use is common among university students, but its associations with sleep hygiene and academic performance remain uncertain. This study examined these associations among Palestinian university students.

Methods

A cross-sectional questionnaire-based study was conducted from March 21 to May 28, 2026. Among 379 participants, continuous grade point average (GPA) was available for 354. Measures included estimated caffeine intake, caffeine timing, Sleep Hygiene Index (SHI) score, sleep duration, sleep regularity, and study hours. Associations were assessed using analysis of variance, correlation, and multivariable linear regression. Caffeine intake was entered into the regression model as ln(mg/day + 1).

Results

The mean age was 20.71 ± 1.98 years, and 50.1% were female. Mean Sleep Hygiene Score was 23.32 ± 8.34, with acceptable internal consistency (Cronbach’s α = 0.775). Estimated caffeine intake averaged 253.5 ± 180.9 mg/day, with a median of 223 mg/day. Sleep Hygiene Score was positively correlated with raw caffeine intake (Pearson r = .282, p < .001; Spearman rho = .310, p < .001) and log-transformed intake (Pearson r = .210, p < .001). Mean GPA was 3.03 ± 0.59. No statistically significant association was detected between GPA and caffeine category (p = .584), log-transformed caffeine intake (r = −.084, p = .116), raw caffeine intake (Spearman rho = −.098, p = .066), or Sleep Hygiene Score (r = −.061, p = .249). In multivariable regression (n = 352, adjusted R² = 0.123), study hours, sleep regularity, sleep duration, academic year, academic major, and smoking status were independently associated with GPA; caffeine intake was not (B = −0.026, 95% CI [−0.071, 0.020], p = .270).

Conclusion

Higher estimated caffeine intake was associated with poorer sleep hygiene. No statistically significant association with GPA was detected, although the confidence interval does not exclude a negative association. The cross-sectional design limits causal interpretation.
